text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementPaleontologyNeanderthals Were Adept Woodworkers TooBut most of their work has been lostJCBy Jake Currie1:00 PM CDT on October 7, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleThe traditional Neanderthal stereotype might be that of a club-wielding caveman, but they actually had some pretty sophisticated technology. Our archaic cousins fashioned all manner of delicate instruments out of flakes of flint and other stone, including scrapers, axes, knives—even dentist drills. Of course, that’s not the extent of the Neanderthal toolkit, only what survived to be scrutinized by us tens of thousands of years later. Most Neanderthal wooden tools have unfortunately been lost to the ravages of time—with a few exceptions. Powered By 10 ShareNextStayAbric Romaní, a cliffside settlement in Spain occupied by Neanderthals around 70,000 to 39,000 years ago, contains evidence of wooden objects preserved by travertine incrustation. During this process, calcium carbonate builds up around the wood, which decays, leaving an impression so detailed it’s possible to make out individual plant cells.
